news.title: Concacaf W Championship: Chelsea players, fixtures and World Cup qualifying explained
news.body_en: Three Chelsea Women players will represent their countries at the 2026 Concacaf W Championship, with Alyssa Thompson, Kadeisha Buchanan and Becky Spencer all hoping to help their nations qualify for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup. The tournament begins on Friday 27 November and has taken on added significance, as it will also determine Concacaf’s places at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles and the next World Cup in Brazil. Here is everything you need to know about the tournament, including the Chelsea players involved, their fixtures and how qualification works. Three Blues are set to feature in the tournament, representing the United States, Canada and Jamaica. Alyssa Thompson is part of the United States squad, with Naomi Girma remaining at Chelsea to continue her recovery from injury. Thompson will hope to feature when the defending champions face El Salvador in their quarter-final. Kadeisha Buchanan is included in Canada's squad for their last-eight meeting with Panama, while Becky Spencer will represent Jamaica as they take on Costa Rica. All three of our players are scheduled to feature in quarter-final action at the Texas Health Mansfield Stadium. Jamaica face Costa Rica on Friday 27 November, with kick-off at 10pm UK time. A victory would secure Jamaica's place at the 2027 Women's World Cup and keep their hopes of qualifying for the 2028 Olympic Games alive. The United States take on El Salvador in the early hours of Saturday 28 November, with kick-off at 1.30am UK time. The USWNT will be looking to make home advantage count as they begin their bid to retain the Concacaf title and secure another World Cup appearance. As the 2026 Olympic Games host, the USA have an automatic berth in the Los Angeles games. Canada meet Panama on Saturday 28 November, with kick-off at 6pm UK time. Buchanan and her team-mates know that victory would guarantee their place at the World Cup, with the potential for two further matches to follow as the knockout competition progresses. The 2026 Concacaf W Championship features eight nations: the USA, Canada, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Haiti, Jamaica, Mexico and Panama. The USA and Canada qualified automatically as the confederation's two highest-ranked teams, while the remaining six nations earned their places by winning their qualifying groups. The tournament follows a single-game knockout format, beginning with four quarter-final matches. The winners progress to the semi-finals, followed by a third-place match and the final. The quarter-final match-ups were determined by the FIFA Women's World Rankings, with the highest-ranked team facing the lowest-ranked side in the opening round. The USA are reigning champions and have won the past three editions of the tournament, as well as nine in total, with Canada the only other nation to lift the trophy, doing so twice. The tournament takes place from 27 November to 5 December, with matches split between the Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Mansfield and the Shell Energy Stadium in Houston. The 2026 Concacaf W Championship doubles as the qualifying competition for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil. Concacaf has four direct World Cup places, with all four quarter-final winners automatically qualifying for the tournament. The four nations beaten in the quarter-finals still have a chance to reach the tournament, through the FIFA Women's World Cup play-offs. Those four teams will contest two-legged matches on Wednesday 2 December, with the winners securing Concacaf’s two places in the second phase of the inter-confederation play-offs. They will then compete alongside four other nations for three remaining World Cup places, with the six teams drawn into three knockout pathways in February 2027. That means Concacaf could have up to six representatives at the 2027 Women's World Cup. The tournament also determines Concacaf's qualification places for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. The two finalists and the third-place team will secure spots at the women's Olympic football tournament. However, the United States have already qualified automatically as hosts. If the USWNT finish in the top three, the final Concacaf Olympic place will go to the team finishing fourth. We will keep you updated on how our players fare throughout the tournament on the Chelsea Official App and website.

news.title: Alonso urges focus and concentration ahead of Nottingham Forest
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso has challenged his team to show greater focus, concentration and intensity when they face Nottingham Forest, with the manager demanding an improved performance from his players at the City Ground on Friday night. The Blues return to Premier League action looking to respond after Saturday's disappointment, with Alonso keen to see a reaction from everyone involved as we attempt to get back to winning ways. The manager wants us to produce a more competitive display against Forest, with particular emphasis on our approach and application throughout the game, which he believes will bring positive results. 'I want a high focus game, high concentration game with intensity, very connected, very knowing what's going on, and we are working for that,' Alonso said. 'But we are not there yet. We want to show a much better game today. We want to show another kind of level of performance, competitive level, a reaction from everyone.' Alonso also reflected on the progress Chelsea have made in developing their mentality this season, acknowledging some difficult moments along the way. He believes the overall trend is positive, but stressed the team must keep improving and maintain the expected standards more consistently. 'I think that the tendency is improving, but we have highs and lows, and I think that we knew that could happen,' he explained. 'But when you feel it, it's not good to have that bad feeling that we had on Saturday, for sure. 'Having lived that, we have talked about what we can do better and what we have to do better. There are no excuses not to do better. There are things that we all can do, even if you have a bad day or in terms of feeling some things that you have to do at this level. 'We are in the process. I think that it's taking steps. It's taking a step forward until it is totally in the DNA of the team. It takes time.' Alonso also accepted responsibility for the team's performances, insisting that everyone at the club must work together to ensure Chelsea respond positively against Forest. He knows not everything is within our control, but he believes the team's preparation, focus and approach are in our own hands and can lead us back to winning ways. 'I take the whole responsibility of the team, of how they perform, and we are in this together for sure,' he continued. 'The feeling of the last game is not good, but now it's about looking forward and showing a reaction. There are no excuses. There are no ifs or buts. It's just certain things that we have to do. 'After, the result you can't control, but how you approach the game, what your focus is, what your priority is, that we can define on the training pitch, with the messages and the ideas on how to play the game. 'So we need to show that tomorrow. Not just talk, talk is cheap. It's about showing and performing on the pitch.'

news.title: Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea | Focused on three points
Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea: All you need to know
news.body_en: Chelsea and Nottingham Forest have the chance to lay down an early marker in the first game of the Premier League weekend. Club historian Rick Glanvill and club statistician Paul Dutton look ahead to the 8pm Friday night kick-off at the City Ground. The match pairs the top-flight’s second-worst home side with the tenth-best on the road. Chelsea's only previous outing in this time slot this season was the defeat at Brentford back in August and the Blues will be determined to make amends for last weekend’s 4-1 home to loss rivals Leeds United. Oliver Glasner’s hosts claimed their only home spoils of the season so far with victory over Manchester City earlier this month, but then lost 2-0 at Bournemouth last weekend to revive concerns about their future in the top flight. Xabi Alonso’s men, who slipped to eighth as a result of the set-back against Leeds, now face successive games against bottom-four clubs – with Crystal Palace coming to Stamford Bridge on Wednesday. A fifth win in six league visits to the banks of the Trent would lift the Blues back into the UEFA places with just over two-thirds of the league season remaining. Ahead of our trip to the City Ground, Alonso confirmed that this game would be too soon for Joao Pedro or Maxence Lacroix to make their return to the pitch, although Moises Caicedo is available to feature, despite being forced off in the first half of last week's game against Leeds. ‘Moi has been able to train and he is going to be okay for tomorrow,' said our manager, in his pre-match press conference at Cobham on Thursday afternoon. ‘For Maxence, it's one less week than from the last game, so we are closer in his recovery, but not for this game.’ First visited in October 1906, the City Ground was once a place of dread for Chelsea fans, engendered by 6-0 and 7-0 losses in the late 1970s and early 1990s. Since defeat there in 1997, though, the Blues have remained unbeaten in five visits, winning four of them. In February 1999, former Blues goalie Dave Beasant conceded a Scandinavian treble – an opener from young Finland frontman Mikael Forssell, then two from Denmark midfielder Bjarne Goldbaek, in a 3-1 win. Two months later Forest were relegated, but they returned to the top flight in 2022 after a two-decade absence. The Blues’ first visit for almost 24 years, on New Year’s Day 2023, finished 1-1 with Raheem Sterling breaking the deadlock before Serge Aurier restored parity.  The result ended a four-game winless run on the road under Graham Potter. Chelsea passed the 900 Premier League away goals mark in May the following year, in a topsy-turvy affair on the south bank of the River Trent. The lead changed hands three times, with Mykhailo Mudryk breaking the deadlock eight minutes in. Willy Boly levelled minutes later and, with a quarter-hour to go, Callum Hudson-Odoi edged his new side ahead against his old team-mates.  The final ten minutes saw substitutions pay off, as Sterling equalised and Reece James crossed for Nicolas Jackson’s winner. A year later, the 100th meeting between the two sides across all competitions at the season’s close was settled by Levi Colwill’s goal early in the second half. Most recently, in October 2025, Chelsea claimed a third-straight league win at the City Ground for the first time with an emphatic 3-0 victory, in which Josh Acheampong’s header, a Pedro Neto free-kick and James’ emphatic volley sealed the points. This match showcases the Premier League teams with the highest share of goals scored in the opening 15 minutes – Chelsea (seven of 20 goals, or 35 per cent) and Nottingham Forest (three of nine, 33 per cent). To date, neither side has conceded in that timeframe. The Blues have the highest shooting accuracy in the top flight this term (40 per cent) while Nottingham Forest have the worst (20.4 per cent). Against Leeds, Emmanuel Emegha became the second Chelsea player to find the net at the Bridge on his first league start. Jordan Henderson did likewise two minutes into his debut against Bournemouth in October. Nottingham Forest coach Glasner has drawn his last two encounters with Chelsea 1-1. His side have failed to score in a division-high six matches this season. Last weekend’s 2-0 loss at Bournemouth was also the second time this season Nottingham Forest failed to register a shot on target in the opening hour of a league game.

news.title: OTD: Rare John Terry brace helps Chelsea thump Charlton
news.body_en: Chelsea travelled to The Valley on 27 November 2004 and the performance and result that followed against Charlton Athletic proved another indicator of our title credentials that season. Jose Mourinho’s Blues made the short journey to south-east London two points clear of nearest rivals Arsenal and with our most recent away games, 4-1 wins at West Brom and Fulham respectively, fresh in the mind. Chelsea lined up in the customary 4-3-3 formation favoured by Mourinho that season and didn’t take long to get into our groove. Eidur Gudjohnsen dropped deep and played an incisive pass into the path of Damien Duff, who held off Paul Konchesky and finished neatly from a tight angle. Ricardo Carvalho headed against his own bar but that was about as close as the Addicks came all afternoon. We put our foot down at the start of the second half and captain John Terry netted twice in three minutes to make sure the points would be heading back west. Both goals stemmed from right-sided, inswinging Duff corners. Terry planted a header home from the first and then prodded in his second after Carvalho kept the ball alive. Terry would end his glittering Chelsea career with 67 goals – and this was one of only two occasions he scored more than once in a game, the other coming against fellow capital outfit Fulham in April 2013. Gudjohnsen added the cherry on top of the cake with a trademark dinked finish from Lampard’s bending through ball. The 4-0 scoreline did not flatter the Blues, who moved five points clear at the top of the table. Arsenal’s loss at Liverpool the following day ensured it was a lead we would not relinquish, going on to win our first Premier League title a few months later.

news.title: Alonso on utilising Emegha’s power and handling 'chaotic situations'
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso has highlighted the qualities Emmanuel Emegha brings to the Blues' frontline as we prepare for what he expects to be another tough physical challenge against Nottingham Forest. Emegha made his first Premier League start for Chelsea against Leeds United last time out. Although the game ended in defeat, there was plenty to like about the Dutchman’s combative full debut. He marked the occasion with his first Blues goal to open the scoring and, although it ultimately wasn’t enough to secure a share of the points, Alonso liked what he saw from Emegha. ‘He did really well,’ replied our manager when asked about the striker’s performance ahead of our next Premier League fixture at the City Ground. ‘I think that in the first half we were able to exploit his qualities. He's so powerful. He creates problems for the defenders when he has so much space. ‘He scored a very, very good strike. So it was great for him to have that feeling on his first game, and we need to keep going.’ Those qualities may come in useful for Alonso and the Blues tomorrow evening if Emegha is selected against Forest, with the Blues likely to face a physical battle similar to that posed by Leeds. Our ability to handle the physicality and intensity of many Premier League opponents was another subject Alonso highlighted going into tomorrow's game. ‘That's the standards of the Premier League and for sure it's an important thing that we have spoken about, that we need to do much better,’ he continued. ‘Because if you don't do that, you are not able to control important situations in the game. ‘Analysing and talking about things during this week, it's one for tomorrow, but also one for the rest of the season: we need to be more competitive in that part. If not, we will have problems. But it's clear, and now we need to execute it. ‘You need to be able to deal with chaotic situations, with intense situations when you are playing home or away, when that energy is created. We have experienced that and you need to deal with that because, for sure, those situations will happen. ‘It's very difficult for me, and I found it from the first day, to have absolute control of all the games. You have to be a top, top, top team to reach that, and we need to be able to deal with that.’

news.title: Ibrahim Rabbaj helps Morocco into knockout stage at Under-17 World Cup
news.body_en: Ibrahim Rabbaj and Morocco have made it out of the group stage and into the knockout phase of the FIFA Under-17 World Cup despite a 2-0 defeat to Spain in Qatar on Thursday. After playing every minute of the opening two fixtures, the Blues forward started the third and final group game on the bench, before coming on as a second-half substitute in the 58th minute. His nation were 1-0 down at the time, thanks to an early strike from Ebrima Tunkara, and before Rabbaj had time to impact the match, Spain doubled their lead with a Guillermo Trujillano strike shortly after the hour mark. Rabbaj created two chances for his side after his introduction, but wayward finishing saw Morocco unable to breach the Spanish defence, and ultimately the North African nation fell to defeat. Defeat did not dent Morocco's qualifying hopes, thanks to four points from their opening two matches, and the Atlas Lions finished the group in second spot on goal difference. That was one ahead of China, who saw off Fiji 8-0 in their final group game, but were unable to add the extra goal that would have seen them leapfrog Morocco in the table. Defeating Spain was always going to be a tall order for Morocco, but by defeating Fiji and taking a point from their clash with China, the North Africans had done the hard work that made qualification likely, given that the eight best third-placed teams also progress to the round of 32. Rabbaj and his team-mates will have to wait to see who they face in the knockout phase, with the final group games set for Friday 27 November, when the knockout bracket will take shape.

news.title: Xabi Alonso calls for a 'strong, competitive reaction' at Forest
news.body_en: Xabi Alonso has called on his Chelsea players to come out fighting to return to winning ways at Nottingham Forest, insisting that we must get the basics right first and foremost. The Blues have suffered Premier League defeats to Sunderland and Leeds United either side of the international break, something our manager is not prepared to take lightly. He is determined for his side to fight back and return to form, starting with tomorrow evening’s trip to the City Ground, when he knows the Blues will need to perform at a higher level than last time out against Leeds. ‘For sure, we want to show our reaction,’ said Alonso. ‘We want to show that we can do much better. ‘That's been the main focus and the goal for tomorrow because we are expecting a tough game, and we need to be competitive and to show that tomorrow.’ During his pre-match press conference, it was put to Alonso whether the absence of players like Joao Pedro and Moises Caicedo – who was forced off with an injury during the first half against Leeds – has contributed to our disappointing results. The Spaniard dismissed that notion, putting the Leeds defeat down to a drop in our performance across the board, which he knows will always be punished by Premier League sides. He said: ‘There were many reasons [for the Leeds defeat]. Football reasons, things that we can't afford, things that basically in football are so important to compete at this level. If you don't get those right, you don't play good. ‘For sure, the idea and the goal and the work and the talks this week have been in that direction, to show a good game and to compete much better tomorrow. ‘If you look at Saturday, we missed not just players, we missed many basics to compete in the game. That's been made clear during the week, talking about how we need those basics in football to compete, and to know what it takes to be ready for each game. For sure, we will need that tomorrow. ‘Especially, we missed it in the second half against Leeds, but that's behind us now. It's analysed, but we don't forget that game. My idea is that we don't forget what we did and that in the future we say those are the standards that we can't afford because they were not acceptable at this level.’ That means Alonso and his squad have their sights set on one thing: producing an improved performance and claiming all three points the next time we step onto the pitch, against Nottingham Forest. ‘It's not what we've done, it's what we can do,' he concluded. 'We need our focus to be about the games that we have done better against these kinds of teams, and how when you don't do it, you don't show the good level. ‘That's why the main thing tomorrow is a strong reaction, a hard reaction, a competitive reaction. We need to show tomorrow.’

news.title: Alonso Press Conference 🎙️
Xabi Alonso confirms Chelsea team news for Nottingham Forest
news.body_en:
Xabi Alonso has confirmed Moises Caicedo is fit to feature against Nottingham Forest tomorrow and delivered the latest on Maxence Lacroix and Joao Pedro.
 The Blues are on the road tomorrow evening as we travel to the City Ground, and we will be looking to shake off the disappointment of our last outing against Leeds United. A subplot of that defeat was an injury Caicedo sustained in the opening 45 minutes, the Ecuadorian midfielder being forced off after landing heavily while challenging for a header. However, Alonso confirmed at his pre-match press conference at Cobham this afternoon that Caicedo is back in contention. ‘Yes [he has been able to train this week] and he is going to be okay for tomorrow,' replied Alonso when asked about Caicedo's fitness. Alonso was also questioned on Joao Pedro's recovery from a thigh injury. The Brazilian hasn't featured since our win over Everton in October, and the Blues manager confirmed the striker isn't returning tomorrow evening against Forest. Lacroix also remains sidelined with the hamstring issue sustained during our Carabao Cup tie against Liverpool in October. ‘It’s one less week than from the last game,' Alonso explained, when asked if the France international was getting close to making a comeback.  'So we are closer in his recovery, but not for this game.’

news.title: Chavarria: We're going to treat it like it's the last game we play
news.body_en: Pep Chavarria says he and his Chelsea team-mates are a family that will give everything against Nottingham Forest tomorrow to live up to the ‘honour’ and ‘responsibility’ of representing the Blues. The Spaniard arrived in west London during the summer, completing a switch from Rayo Vallecano, having risen through the league system to the top of the pyramid in his homeland. He is adapting to the different demands posed by Premier League football, which were demonstrated by the tough opponents we faced in our last two matches: Sunderland and Leeds United. However, the challenge is one the full-back is relishing and one he expected when he jumped at the chance to join Chelsea. ‘It is certainly true that they are, for me, two completely different leagues,’ said Chavarria. ‘I think the Spanish league has a bit more control, a bit more tactical. Here, the Premier League is everything fused together. Here, it is more physical, more technical; the matches are sometimes crazier. ‘It's a league with a lot of intensity, where any team can win, so you have to be ready for absolutely everything. In the end, I also see that it's a league where there are constantly duels, where you have to overcome the opposing team and see who comes out on top. ‘I knew what to expect, because it's true that the Premier League suits my game better, and I'm a player who really likes being intense, going into challenges, being aggressive. ‘So I expected it would be a very tough league, but until you arrive and play the matches, you don't truly realise where you are. So, for me, it's the best league in the world right now.’ That adaptation process has been helped by the quality of the team-mates Chavarria has found around him at Cobham, explaining he couldn’t have asked for any more from his fellow Blues and manager Xabi Alonso. ‘It was incredible with my team-mates, they gave me an amazing welcome,’ he continued. ‘When I arrived, for example, I crossed paths with Reece James, and Reece is an incredible captain who has helped me so much. ‘All my team-mates have helped me a lot, and above all, Moi (Caiced) has also helped me fit in really well. At the beginning, when I was learning English, the two of us were speaking Spanish and he helped me with a lot of things. ‘But to tell you the truth, I see that my team-mates are like a family. We're all there to help each other, and honestly I'm very happy because I have a good relationship with everyone and we have a good time. ‘Xabi's one of the best coaches in the world, and both he and the staff help us a lot. We have a lot of solutions, and it's a real honour because finding this quality of work is very difficult in football, and we have it, so we're very happy. ‘They always ask you to learn new things or things you need to improve, and I think I'm learning a lot, and I think I'm adapting quickly to what this league is, because here if you don't adapt quickly, they don't wait for you. ‘So I'm trying to give my absolute best. I know I can give a lot more, but they are helping me a lot, and I think that in these matches that progression is going to show.’ However, he knows the need to show that progression as the Blues look to bounce back from defeats to Sunderland and Leeds either side of the international break. The chance to do so comes tomorrow evening, when we take on Forest at the City Ground in the Premier League, and the Spaniard is clear he and his team-mates will give everything to take all three points and make up for the disappointment of our last game. ‘We have to give a lot more because in the end we're at a club where the demands are at a different level,’ Chavarria continued. ‘We know the responsibility we have and I think we've realised that we can't repeat a match like that again. ‘Obviously, on any given day we can win, we can lose, or we can draw, but the attitude we had, I think, wasn't right, and we players know that it was our fault. So we're already mentally focused on going all out with the bit between our teeth. ‘We're going to treat Nottingham Forest like it's the last game we play, and we truly believe it, we take it seriously. That's the only way, because football now is so competitive that any team can beat you. We are clear that we want to work and we want to be a competitive team, so the only way forward is to stay united and work even harder. ‘I think it will be like these last two games we had against Sunderland and Leeds – very physical teams playing with a back five, playing very directly, with very powerful and quality players up front. ‘Ultimately, it will be a hard-fought match with a lot of individual duels, decided by small details like most games are, and we have to stay extremely focused so that we land the first blow.’

news.title: Bjorn back stronger than ever for club and country
news.body_en: As Sweden gear up for their FIFA Women's World Cup qualifier against Scotland next week, they’ll be buoyed by having a fit and firing Nathalie Bjorn ready to go. The centre-back had a tough time with injuries last season, missing three months with a hamstring problem at the start of the year before suffering a set-back just 120 seconds into her comeback appearance for Chelsea in March. But after another six months away from first-team football, the 29-year-old is back and finding form as she prepares to try and book Sweden’s place at the 2027 Women’s World Cup. It’s not been an easy road, as she admitted recently. And while a physical injury also tests a player psychologically, the Swedish star said she has grown stronger mentally before putting together a string of positive performances on the pitch against Charlton Athletic, Hacken and Paris Saint-Germain in recent weeks. ‘It was really difficult,’ Nathalie said on the mental side of dealing with back-to-back injuries. ‘Obviously, my team-mates of course really helped me. ‘My physio really helped me and they have supported me, and I've got so much from them. And then mentally just you have to work with yourself in different ways, and I have a great support system around me. ‘So they, my family, fiancee, friends, all helped me. But some of it comes from within also. So it's been a mental struggle. ‘You need to learn how to work after that, and you take it as learnings and you learn so much about yourself, and you realise why you love this game and that you never want to take it for granted again. ‘So I'm also grateful for having these set-backs to be even stronger mentally and physically.  I feel already stronger. I feel mentally I'm in a much stronger place than I think I've ever been coming back from these two injuries. ‘It all gets to the test and see where you're at and how much you can grow when you need to learn, and every day hasn't been all flowery and sunshine. It's been really tough days, but I made it through those days, and for that I'm very proud of myself.’ Bjorn also spoke about leadership and becoming a stronger team alongside Chelsea vice-captain Lucy Bronze in the latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast. Lucy explained what Nathalie does behind the scenes which can be so important to the club: 'It’s easy sometimes to drive a standard, but keeping these players in the right place and making sure everyone’s always together and there’s not a person dropping off, that's what Nat does. 'Nat’s the one who’s always bringing them back together, bringing everyone together, always positive, always a good vibe.' A place at the World Cup is at stake, and Sweden will be hoping with Bjorn’s help they can reach the finals in South America to improve on their third-place finish last time out in 2023.

news.body_en: Ibrahim Rabbaj and Morocco remain in contention for a place in the knockout stages of the FIFA Under-17 World Cup ahead of their final group fixture against Spain. The Chelsea forward has featured in both of Morocco's opening matches in Qatar, helping his side collect four points from their first two outings. Morocco began their campaign with a 6-0 victory against Fiji, with Rabbaj making an incredible impact. The 17-year-old scored and assisted, alongside winning a penalty in the second half. That was followed by a 2-2 draw versus China, leaving the north Africans second in Group H heading into the final round of matches. Rabbaj has played every minute across the opening two fixtures, causing real problems for opposition defences down the right wing. He has registered five key passes, 12 touches in the opposition box and 35 progressive carries throughout the tournament so far, highlighting his impact for the Atlas Lions. Rabbaj’s side head into their final group-stage match against Spain knowing a draw would guarantee progression to the Round of 32. Their four-point haul already leaves them well placed to advance as one of the best third-placed teams. The final group fixture kicks off at 3pm (UK time) on Thursday 26 November and will determine whether Morocco's Under-17 World Cup journey continues into the knockout rounds, with Rabbaj aiming to help fire his nation into the next stage of the tournament.

news.title: Training gallery: Focused on Forest
Inside the life of Becky Spencer
news.body_en: We get to know Blues goalkeeper Becky Spencer better in our feature asking the Chelsea Women players about their early days in the game and their interests away from the pitch. Spencer is currently preparing for a huge game for Jamaica, who take on Costa Rica on Friday evening with a place at the 2027 Women's World Cup on the line. It is the latest chapter in a footballing journey that began 30 years ago now... I grew up in north-west London, a place called Harrow. I'm one of five, so I lived with three of my sisters and my brother. It was really nice. I had a good childhood. At what age did you first start playing football? I want to say five. Three of my sisters played football. I'm the youngest, and they all played in the same team. And I used to play for Wembley under-10s, but obviously they were in the seniors. So on a Saturday I would have my little seven-a-side games, and then on the Sunday I would go to the senior game. By the time they were retiring, football hadn't turned pro yet. This was in the nineties. So they kind of paved the way for me to be next. What was the name of your first grassroots team? How old were you when you first joined an academy? I grew up at Arsenal Academy. I was there from the age of nine until 22. Who would you say has been the biggest influence on your football career to date? I think it's just my family in general. I said that all of my sisters played. My brother also did play football, but my parents have obviously been around for all of that, so they took them to football and then they continued to take me to football afterwards. And you know, they put a lot of work in and a lot of sacrifice into making sure that I got to go for numerous years and travelling to places. What's your biggest career highlight to date? I've got quite a few to be honest, but I would say being at the World Cup with Jamaica, definitely. Who are your best friends in football? My friend Rosella Ayane. She's an old Chelsea player, and then I played at Tottenham for six years. She plays for Morocco, but yeah, we met at Tottenham. We always knew each other, but we met and we bonded straight away. And I'd say that she's one of my best friends. Also Drew Spence, another Chelsea player. I've known Drew for years and years, and then we just ended up playing in the same team throughout our careers, which you are lucky to do. We always take that for granted. Playing with your best mates is something that you never really think you're going to do. When you do, it's just like: ‘This is amazing’. Can you name your top three favourite players of all time? There’s a Valencia goalkeeper called Santiago Canizares. I used to love his style when I was younger. He used to have bleached blonde hair. When I was younger, I used to try and dress like him when I was playing and tuck my shirt in, wear his boots. I thought I’m nothing like him, but I just really enjoyed watching him. I'd say Rachel Yankee is one of my favourites. Also, I had the pleasure of playing with her, and she's now like one of my really really good friends. On and off the pitch, she's just one of my favourite people. And maybe Xavi from Barcelona. Definitely bought a shirt with his name on. It was one of those knock-off ones that you get on holiday. And I was like, 'I want his name on the back of mine' so my mum was like ‘let’s go to the shop’. By the time I got home, it was literally peeling off. When I was at the academy I had Spenny. That didn’t last long. Then I had 50 Spence. That didn’t carry on! What do you like to do most away from football? I’m quite introverted, so I like to have just time on my own. I’m a family person. I've got a little niece, she's so cute. So on days off, I'll go and see her and see if I can look after her for the day. On a Friday, we have this thing where my family still go to my parents' house. So we'll all congregate there on a Friday, have a meal, and just sit there and just chat about what everyone's been doing. Are you watching any TV series at the moment? I've just finished a couple, but I'm into reading at the moment. I’m reading Colleen Hoover, I’ve just finished Verity and I’m going onto Ugly Love now. If we looked at your Spotify playlist, who would be dominating your most-played artists? I'd say Olivia Dean. I put her album on and just let that play out at the moment What are your top three holiday destinations, either that you've been to already or you would like to go to? I would say Turks and Caicos. I went there just before the World Cup, lovely. I've just come back from Greece, so I went to Crete. That would be one of the best. And I'd say Jamaica. I haven't been to Jamaica on holiday, though, I always go to play or whatever. But I'll say Jamaica. I love going back there. If you had guests over for dinner, what would you cook for them? I’m not a very good cook! I'll try and do a seafood linguine. I’ll try! Garlic bread on the side, maybe a little side salad. Can you tell the fans something that they might not know about you? I made my professional debut when I was 14 at Arsenal. Sunderland away, my parents had dropped me to the training ground. The manager at the time was Vic Akers, he went and spoke to my parents, so they knew and then he called me. It was a freezing day up in Sunderland, not many people there. What's the best piece of advice you've ever received? I got some advice from Rachel Yankee. She said to me one time, ‘when you know, you know’. I think I've used it with loads of different things that I've done now. At my age, I think you've got to make some really important decisions, that’s made me also process things differently. It’s good advice. What does football mean to you? It means everything. I've never really been without it. I think when you are without it, even in the summer, you miss it. I think it's being around people. Also, having your own identity within a big group, it means everything because that's all I've ever known.

news.title: The Dave Sexton story
Made in Cobham: Heze Grimwade
news.body_en: Midfielder Heze Grimwade has grown up at Cobham, and the Chelsea Academy prospect reflects on the family support, hard work and determination that have shaped his journey so far. From playing up an age group to spending extra hours working on his game, the Academy midfielder has always approached football with a clear sense of purpose. ‘It was always football. I have never wanted to do anything else, I’ve always been passionate. When I signed here I was so, so happy.’ Heze Grimwade’s unwavering focus on football has been shaped by a close-knit family environment, both at Cobham and at home. It’s an environment that has provided the support and structure for him to pursue his dreams from an early age. Born in Woolwich and growing up across south-east London, Grimwade has always been surrounded by his large family. The oldest of eight children, with two brothers and five sisters, he has grown up with the responsibility of setting an example for his younger siblings both on and off the pitch. Family has always been at the centre of his upbringing. Grimwade reveals that his parents made a conscious decision to structure their working lives around being present and homeschooling the 16-year-old and his siblings. That support has extended into his football, with his father being particularly influential in helping him pursue his ambitions. ‘My parents don’t work nine-to-five jobs because they want to be there for us,’ says Grimwade. ‘They have always been so involved with my career – my Dad is at every game and I’ve only missed one training session throughout my entire time with Chelsea. ‘Mum and Dad are always there and ready to support me. There have been sacrifices and I’m very grateful for what they’ve done for us.’ For Grimwade, football was always the ambition. He remembers attending sessions at Chelsea at the age of four and playing against much older children in his Sunday League matches at the weekend, even as a six-year-old. Having joined at such a young age, Chelsea has been a constant throughout almost all Grimwade’s life. He believes the club has played a significant role in shaping him, especially socially, having been homeschooled. The friendships the midfielder has developed at Cobham helped him develop and he credits the people around him with influencing his humour, confidence and personality. Grimwade has also become accustomed to playing above his age group. Having regularly played and training with older players since his early years, he has never placed too much importance on his age. ‘I don’t think about my age, I just focus on my ability and getting better every day. I don’t mind what type of match I play in, I just pray and ask God to guide me to make the right decisions, play with confidence and have enough energy to work for the whole game.’ That mentality has continued as he has progressed through the age groups, with the opportunity to train alongside older players providing further motivation. His biggest influences throughout his development at Chelsea has been the coaches who have worked with Grimwade across several age groups. Grimwade’s footballing development has involved various memorable moments over the years, but his favourite came against Bayern Munich in the KDB Cup back in 2025. He told us: ‘I missed a penalty earlier in that game and then we went down to ten men. We were drawing and then I scored a free-kick to win the game.’ Confidence has never been something he’s struggled with, and he emphasises that he approaches games with the intention to enjoy himself rather than allowing the occasions to overwhelm him. That confidence is also reflected in his approach to training. Grimwade’s routine extends to additional running and gym work often taking place on his off days. Away from football, Grimwade’s life is largely centred around family. His days are structured around training, extras and recovery, before returning home to spend time with his siblings. He is also someone who values routine, sticking to a bedtime of 7.30pm to allow him to recover fully and go again every day. There is a creative side to his family too, as his mother used to sing. Grimwade says: ‘All us kids can sing to a decent level, and our house is a house full of rhythm. We love music!’ For someone who has spent almost his entire life at Chelsea, his ambitions remain clear: to compete for the biggest honours in the game. The young Blue is proud of the journey that has brought him to this point but recognises there is still plenty of work to do. His focus remains on improving physically, developing his game and continuing to make the most of the opportunities around him. ‘I’m proud of myself and the journey so far, but I know there’s still a lot of work to do and I’m looking forward to it.’

news.title: N'Golo Kante's best Chelsea strikes!
news.body_en: On the day N'Golo Kante returns to Stamford Bridge to play in the Champions League, we have looked back at the goals the midfielder scored for Chelsea and picked out five of our favourites. Kante, now 35, currently plays his football in Turkey with Fenerbahce. They take on Shakhtar Donetsk in the league phase of the Champions League this evening, with the game in SW6 because the Ukrainian side are calling the Bridge home for their European football this term. During seven hugely successful and trophy-laden years at Chelsea between 2016 and 2023, Kante cemented his status as one of the world's top midfielders. While his game revolved more around cute positioning, destructive defensive work and bursts upfield than goalscoring, Kante still netted some spectacular strikes in blue. Here are five of the best, which are sure to bring back some happy memories... Kante’s first ever Blues goal is one to remember, with his sublime right-footed effort one of four Chelsea goals in our 4-0 win over the Red Devils. The Frenchman finished off a lovely move after Cesar Azpilicueta and Pedro combined well. The latter audaciously flicked the ball into Kante’s path before he danced through the visitors' defence and finished with aplomb. The midfielder cleverly slowed his run to latch onto an Eden Hazard cutback and thump a finish into the roof of the net against the champions Man City, on our way to a 2-0 Premier League victory in December 2018. A few weeks later, N'Golo somehow nutmegged three Tottenham players with a shot in the second leg of our League Cup semi-final tie with Tottenham. His sweet half-volley skipped into the net, with visiting keeper Paulo Gazzaniga the last to be bamboozled. Kante marked his return after injury by getting us back into the game against Liverpool with a stunning strike from the edge of the box. The Frenchman drifted in with the ball from the right, skipped past two Liverpool players before slamming his shot beyond Alisson and into the top corner. Kante exhibited his ability to find the corner of the goal throughout his Blues career, and nowhere was that more evident than with his low strike beyond Kasper Schmeichel with his weaker foot in a 3-0 win at the home of his former employers Leicester City.

news.title: OTD: Schalke v Chelsea | 25 November 2014
Terry Venables: A born leader remembered
news.body_en: Three years on from the sad passing of former Blues captain Terry Venables aged 80 on 25 November 2023, we remember why he will always have a place in the hearts of everyone at Chelsea. Terry Venables might be better known as the manager who almost led England to European Championship glory during a summer when football ‘came home’, but to an older generation of Chelsea fans, he will forever be the larger-than-life captain of Tommy Docherty’s Diamonds, the moniker bestowed upon the promising group of players coming through at Stamford Bridge in the early 1960s. It was quite the coup for the Blues to bring him to west London in the first place, as the Dagenham-born youngster was coveted by clubs throughout the capital during his school days. Chelsea finally secured the services of the boyhood Tottenham fan, just as they did with so many of the capital’s top talents around that time, thanks in no small part to the work of the larger-than-life club scout Jimmy Thompson and the clear pathway established between the Blues’ youth set-up and the first team. ‘Chelsea had a good name for bringing young kids through,’ Venables told Rick Glanvill for our official historian’s book Rhapsody in Blue. ‘Even as a kid you’re ambitious: you thought you’d get into the team at 17 or 18.’ He did just that, less than two years after arriving for his first day at the club in July 1958 alongside, among others, Peter Bonetti, Allan Harris, Bert Murray and Bobby Tambling. Harris and Murray were two he had struck up a firm friendship with on the schoolboy football scene; it was no coincidence the three of them ended up at the same club. His leadership qualities were spotted early on as he was made captain of a youth team which won back-to-back FA Youth Cups. It was during the first of those triumphs that Venables both started training with the first team and was given his senior Blues debut, which came in February 1960 when he was aged 17. Ted Drake’s side were beaten 4-2 by West Ham United at Upton Park, squandering a two-goal lead in the process. ‘I think it’s fair to say I could have had a better start to my career, with nothing I tried seeming to work for me,’ Venables wrote of the game in his autobiography, Born to Manage. He had started alongside Johnny Brooks, the former Tottenham Hotspur inside-forward who Venables had idolised and subsequently wished to emulate in terms of his composure, charisma and capability of splitting the opposition defence with a slide-rule pass. While that was the only first-team appearance Venables made that term, his attention switched back to the FA Youth Cup, which we won for the first time in 1960 before retaining it the following year. By this time, he had become a regular in the senior Blues set-up, although ‘senior’ may have been a stretch; Drake’s Ducklings, as our title-winning manager’s young charges were known, started the campaign with a side boasting an average age of 24, a number which had decreased to 22 by its conclusion. The inconsistency – some would say naivety – of youth was apparent by the goals for and against tallies, which read 98 and 100 respectively. It was clear, however, that the club had quite a player on our hands in the form of Venables, who took on the No4 shirt and looked to have all the qualities of a classic on-field general, dictating play from deep and directing players positionally. This was not a youngster lacking in confidence – he had, after all, displayed his showmanship over Christmas during his maiden full campaign in the first team by singing on stage at the Hammersmith Palais. An even younger Chelsea side, shorn of its talismanic frontman Jimmy Greaves, struggled during the 1961/62 season and it was largely an unhappy campaign for Venables as he played only 12 matches. There was the highlight of his first-ever goal in senior football, which came in a heavy defeat at Cardiff City, but after featuring in Drake’s final game as Blues boss, replacement Tommy Docherty called upon Venables only three times as the club dropped down into the Second Division. The following campaign saw the transition from Drake’s Ducklings to Docherty’s Diamonds, with Venables one of the major players as we immediately bounced back to the top flight, playing every minute of our 42 league matches that term. A penalty on the final day – the first of eight successful conversions from the spot in the league during his Blues career – in a handsome victory over Portsmouth secured our return to Division One. Aided by his promotion to spot-kick duties, Venables became a regular name on the score sheet for the remainder of his time at the club, but far more noteworthy at that time was his contribution towards dressing-room harmony. During the 1963/64 season he became club captain, a natural role for a player who was always the life and soul. Nearly all of his team-mates from that time spoke fondly of a man who loved a prank but, more than anything, always had the backs of those he led out onto the pitch every Saturday. ‘Terry was a leader right from the start of his career,’ said team-mate Barry Bridges, who came through during the same era. ‘When he was captain I suppose he was only 19 or 20, but he did more to lead the team than the manager. He was the guvnor on the pitch and it was no surprise to see what he went on to achieve as a football manager himself.’ Venables’ first full season as skipper, in 1964/65, was arguably the best of his time here. Not only did it include his only trophy won as a Blue, it also saw his club form recognised at international level. As a result of the two caps won for the senior side during the space of 49 days during the winter of 1964, he became the first man to be capped by England in schoolboy, youth, amateur, Under-23 and full internationals, although he would never play for his country again. After scoring on the opening day of the campaign against Wolverhampton Wanderers, Venables added two more in consecutive games against Leeds and Arsenal which confirmed us as genuine title challengers. A penalty in the first leg of our League Cup final against Leicester City helped secure the club’s first-ever triumph in a major cup competition, but our bid for a domestic Treble came unstuck in the closing weeks. With Venables and Docherty often at loggerheads – two jocular fellows who loved nothing more than to be the centre of attention – things came to a head with the infamous Blackpool incident, when the skipper was one of eight players sent home from an away trip due to breaking curfew. Though he was one of those to return for the final-day loss at Blackpool, the damage had already been done – both to our title hopes and the relationship between captain and manager, despite a brief reconciliation. Winning the League Cup had gained us entry to the Fairs Cup the following season and the European stage seemed to suit Venables down to the ground. He scored a famous hat-trick against Roma in the opening round, which included a goal which would have been replayed time and time again had it occurred in the modern era. When a free-kick was awarded to the Blues, Venables made a song and dance of counting out 10 yards and then, having reached the wall, spun around to receive the pass before finishing with aplomb. ‘We worked things like that out beforehand,’ he said of that cheeky goal. ‘We were non-stop talking about football, like in the cafe in Fulham Broadway, for hours after training. Talking about what you could do, how you could get better.’ The hat-trick came at the end of a run of eight goals in nine games to begin that season, but he would not score again until March and the underlying problems with Docherty came to a head after our tepid FA Cup semi-final defeat to Sheffield Wednesday, when Venables was among those singled out for criticism by the manager. Unfortunately, the damage this time was irreparable. The beginning of the end came in the away dressing room at the Nou Camp ahead of a Fairs Cup semi-final against Barcelona, when Docherty introduced the players to new signing Charlie Cooke. The story goes, as told by the manager, that Venners decided to test the new boy by throwing the ball to him; Cooke promptly caught it on his instep before juggling the ball, taking it on his neck and then flicking it back to Venables. That game in Catalonia would be his last in Chelsea blue. ‘I think I knew then,’ Venables conceded years later. ‘I got the hint when he was juggling the ball in the corner! Things had got to a bad stage. I didn’t understand at the time, but if someone’s got to go, it’s always the player. I’d always wanted to play for Chelsea and I loved it so much I wanted to be there all my career. I didn’t want to go.’ He left just a fortnight later, joining Tottenham Hotspur for a fee of £80,000 and a year later he was part of the side, along with Greaves, which beat their old team-mates in the FA Cup final. Venables represented two more London clubs, Queens Park Rangers – losing an FA Cup quarter-final against the Blues in 1970 as we went on to lift the trophy for the first time – and Crystal Palace, before bringing down the curtain on his playing career in 1974 and embarking on a new chapter in football as a coach. His last two clubs on the pitch were the first two of his managerial career, which hit new heights in 1984 when he took over at Barcelona. ‘El Tel’, as he was dubbed, brought a hard-nosed 4-4-2 to the Nou Camp, where he was ably assisted by his old Chelsea team-mate Allan Harris, and won La Liga in 1984/85. However, they lost the European Cup final against Steaua Bucharest in Seville the following season. He came home to London to manage Tottenham in 1987 and added another FA Cup triumph to the one from his playing days with the Lilywhites and he was also the last Spurs boss to beat Chelsea, in 1990, before our famous 12-year unbeaten run against our rivals. Following this, Venables was given the honour of leading England at a major championship on home soil, as he was appointed manager two years out from the European Championship. His popular Three Lions side captured the hearts and imagination of the country as they reached the semi-finals of Euro 96 before suffering penalty shootout heartache against Germany. Having left England at the end of the tournament, brief spells managing Australia, Crystal Palace, Middlesbrough and Leeds followed before Venables stepped away from football. The lure of assisting Steve McClaren during his ill-fated tenure in charge of England briefly pulled him back into the game, but both left their jobs with the FA following the failure to qualify for Euro 2008. However, it is for the ability, determination and leadership he demonstrated on the Stamford Bridge pitch that he will forever be remembered at Chelsea.

news.title: Emmanuel Emegha on doing ‘anything to win’ and why Reece James is the ‘best captain’
news.body_en: Emmanuel Emegha announced himself to Chelsea supporters with a brilliant goal against Leeds United on Saturday, offering a glimpse of the qualities he is eager to bring to the Blues. Emegha’s performance and goal was one of the few bright spots of an otherwise disappointing afternoon at Stamford Bridge. The striker’s pace, power and natural finishing ability were all on display, with the Dutchman marking his full Blues debut by opening his account for the club. In a career that has already seen him move from his native Netherlands to Belgium, Austria, France and now England, Emegha has always risen to meet the level required of him. He expects to do the same here, as he told our official matchday programme for the Leeds game. ‘That’s why I know that at Chelsea I can and I will also do it,’ said Emegha. ‘Every player is different. There are some players, you buy them and straight away they are… boom! Me, I always need some time to adapt, and I’ve had a lot of injuries. ‘Now I’m happy that I’m over it and I do everything for my body to stay as fit as possible. I want to stay like this because playing for a big club, you cannot be having these injuries, injuries, injuries. It will not work. ‘I’m a winner, I’m a fighter,’ added Emegha. ‘I would do anything to win. If I need to block a ball with the front of my face, I will do it. I’m quick, I know how to make runs in behind, and I know that I can be a nightmare for all the defenders.’ With his height and pace, it appears Emegha possesses the characteristics required to perform in the Premier League. Despite that, he acknowledged training at Cobham every day and playing in English football has been a real step up from what he has known before. ‘I’m in a room full of such talented players, it’s not normal!’ he explained. ‘Before coming, I knew that I could expect a high level, but I didn’t know that it would be so crazy high. But I’m enjoying it. I’m getting better. I’m learning every single day.’ Emegha’s adaptation to life at Chelsea has been aided by the support network around him. The human touch off the pitch can make a big difference on it, and the 23-year-old has felt warmth and care from day one. He also made a point of singling out the skipper for praise. ‘I don’t think that I’ve worked at a club with so many nice people,’ said Emegha. ‘To be honest, since my first day here, even in the kitchen, the way that they take care of us is next level. ‘I also want to say that Reece James is the best captain I’ve ever had in my whole life. I came to this club and he made me feel comfortable. Reece James… he has won it all, he has seen it all, but he’s still so caring. I don’t know how it is for other players, but Joao [Pedro] said it too. One day we had a meeting and he said the same thing. ‘For me, Reece is the example of a leader. He would come to me and make sure that I felt good. If I had a tough training session, he would come to me and tell me, “It’s normal. Tomorrow is a new day. Forget it and move on.” If I missed an open chance in training, it would be easy to say, “Oh, come on!” But Reece… he thought, “Oh, come on!” but he said, “No, come on. Next one, next one!” And he wasn’t even in my team that session! He made me feel so good.’ And if James's message is to keep looking forward and take the next opportunity, Emegha is certainly intent on doing just that. A version of this article was first published in the Chelsea matchday programme, which you can buy past and future copies of.

news.title: Bjorn and Bronze talk leadership and bouncing back stronger in We Are Chelsea
news.body_en: The latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast features defensive duo Nathalie Bjorn and Lucy Bronze joining us to chat and discuss a wide range of subjects, including their individual styles of leadership and how last season inspired them to come back stronger than ever in 2026/27. The pair are part of a Chelsea Women team enjoying a great campaign so far, sitting two points clear at the top of the Women’s Super League table and on course for direct qualification to the knockout stages of the UEFA Women’s Champions League. The Blues remain undefeated in all competitions with 13 wins from 18 games, having scored 39 goals to just seven conceded, while keeping clean sheets in our last four consecutive fixtures, including vital wins over Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain. That form was just one of the subjects they discuss in the latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast, which you can watch in full below. When asked about that impressive form, Bjorn and Bronze both pointed to the lessons learned during a disappointing 2025/26 season – following a hugely successful debut campaign for head coach Sonia Bompastor – as crucial to coming back stronger than ever. ‘From when Sonia first came in and we had this whole season we went unbeaten and everything is good, and then you have a second year that is worse for us,’ explained Bjorn. ‘Then it is all about how you come out from that, what makes you stronger as a group. Obviously none of us is happy with that season, but also it was good value for us – as a group, as players – to be like: “okay, we need to do this better, we need to have better intensity, we need to do this, this and this”. ‘I think that actually helped us get the team together and be able to perform like this.’ Bronze added: ‘Sometimes transitions are a lot harder, especially our first season everyone was like “wow”. ‘But it’s kind of like a honeymoon phase of everything’s going really well and then suddenly something doesn’t go as well and you don’t have as much to fall back on because it’s new territory, under Sonia especially, and we had to figure a lot of things out. ‘I think that’s what you saw in the second year, which normally you would see in the first season. But I think it worked out well because we still knew as a group that the first season gave us so much confidence that we were a good team, we could win and we could do well. So last year it was like this isn’t forever, this is just us repositioning ourselves, figuring ourselves out to be that team again and to be even better.’ As two of the most experienced members of this Chelsea squad, with well over 200 international caps between them, Bjorn and Bronze both take on vice-captain roles for the Blues, alongside skipper Erin Cuthbert. However, as they explained when asked about the other’s strengths, they have very different approaches to leadership, a variety both feel is important to have within such a diverse squad. Bjorn highlighted the way Bronze leads by example, saying: ‘Obviously Lucy, the way she puts in standards in the sessions, in the games, she’s mentally strong and her physicality. ‘If it’s running down the line and you do a tackle or whatever, she always puts the standards really high. That also shows that people take after her, want to do the same, I think it’s impressive.’ Bronze responded: ‘She’s the person who brings people together. It’s so important for a team. ‘It’s easy sometimes to drive a standard, but keeping these players in the right place and making sure everyone’s always together and there’s not a person dropping off, Nat’s the one who’s always bringing them back together, bringing everyone together, always positive, always a good vibe. ‘So we’ve got a good mix of personalities and things that we bring. The perfect leader doesn’t exist, you need to lean on each other. It’s a big group of players with so many personalities, we have to be able to lean on each other and not think we know everything.’ You can watch Bjorn and Bronze discussing those subjects and many more by watching the latest episode of the We Are Chelsea podcast in full above.

news.title: Seven memorable moments against Nottingham Forest
news.body_en: Chelsea and Nottingham Forest's Premier League history dates back to the competition's very first campaign in 1992/93, and since then there have been plenty of games for us to enjoy against the Reds. As well as league meetings in that time, we have faced Forest on several occasions in domestic cup competitions, and our selection of memorable moments includes some of those. The Blues will be trying to add to this list on Friday evening when we travel to the City Ground, and to whet the appetite we take a trip down memory line... Nottingham Forest had only played four matches back in the top flight after promotion when they came to the Bridge, and Gianfranco Zola gave them a quick lesson on how tough the challenge can be in the Premier League. Very quick, in fact, as there were just 25 seconds on the clock when the Italian opened the scoring on our way to a 2-1 victory. Chelsea won the third of our eight FA Cups in 2000, but we were challenged along the way by Forest. This game was almost a personal challenge for Zola, who had one brilliant chip cleared off the line before being flagged offside when tapping in a team-mate's already goal-bound effort. He made amends when we regrouped in the second half, setting up Frank Leboeuf’s opening goal as we won 2-0 and progressed to the fifth round. Chelsea’s 2017/18 Carabao Cup campaign kicked off against Forest at Stamford Bridge with an emphatic 5-1 win on Willy Caballero’s debut. However, it was Michy Batshuayi who starred. The striker only gave us glimpses of his potential with the Blues, but when he did it tended to be memorable. This wasn’t quite up there with his title-winning goal at West Bromwich Albion, but his first – and only – Chelsea hat-trick was a high point. Spanish duo Alvaro Morata and Cesc Fabregas were both playing their last game for Chelsea when we hosted Nottingham Forest in the 2018/19 FA Cup third round. The latter wore the captain’s armband on his 500th match in English football, but also had a penalty saved. That left it for Morata to save the day on his farewell appearance, scoring twice in the second half for a 2-0 Blues win. There were three games left in the Premier League season when Chelsea travelled to the City Ground in 2023/24 with both sides desperate for the points, Forest in a bid to avoid relegation and the Blues in the race for Europe. We took an early lead but were trailing heading into the last 10 minutes, before Raheem Sterling curled into the bottom corner. Two minutes later, a peach of a Reece James cross allowed Nicolas Jackson to head in and give us a dramatic 3-2 victory. The City Ground hosted our last Premier League game in 2024/25, and what a day it was. Effectively a head-to-head contest in the race for UEFA Champions League qualification, a tense match was decided shortly after half-time when Levi Colwill turned in Pedro Neto’s pass for the only goal of the game. Cue wild celebrations in the away end, Chelsea were back in the Champions League. A few months later, we triumphed in emphatic fashion on the banks of the Trent, emerging 3-0 victors with all the goals scored after the break. The highlight was the opener, nodded into the net by Josh Acheampong for his very first senior Chelsea goal. The grin on his face said it all!

Inside the life of Lola Brown
news.body_en: We ask Lola Brown some quickfire questions to get to know the 19-year-old, so impressive in Chelsea Women's draw with Liverpool, a bit better… What is your favourite pre-match hype song? Noah Kahan at the moment. I know Aggie's a big fan of his too. What's the best concert you've ever been to? Do you prefer beach holidays or city breaks? Beach holidays, but I don't sit still. I’m looking for something to do or I’m in the sea, swimming. What was the last beach holiday you went on? I'd count Australia on tour. We went to Bondi and I went in the sea there! If you were stuck on a desert island, what's the one non-essential thing that you would take with you? If I had a plug, an air fryer. You catch anything out of the sea, and then you just put it in the air fryer. What's your favourite thing to do on a day off? Swimming. Swimming, sauna, coffee. All the relaxing stuff. If you weren't a footballer, what would your ideal career be? An artist. I love art, I did it at school for GCSE, but I also paint on shoes a lot and then give them to people. I did it quite a bit at Palace [during her loan spell] as well, and they gave some to the fans. I gave some away, and then other fans were coming up to me saying: "Can we get some?!" I have two – Virgil van Dijk and Lucy Bronze. What's your favorite goal that you've ever scored? I'd say in the 21s, we went to a tournament in Paris and played Bayern Munich in the final, and it was 1-0 when I scored. I still remember it. Scoring at the World Sevens was really good as well. Tell us one thing about you that the fans might not know. I'd say my art again. I love painting. I do it all the time. That's another thing I'm always doing on my day off.

PGA Division 1 report: Chelsea Women Under-18s 10-2 Birmingham City
news.body_en: Chelsea Women’s Under-18s, who play in Division 1 of the PGA Women’s Under-21 League, produced a dominant display at Kingsmeadow on Sunday, scoring ten goals against Birmingham City. Despite conceding inside the opening minute, the Blues responded impressively, netting three times shortly before the break and then adding seven more goals after the interval. Seven different Chelsea players got on the scoresheet, with the result extending our unbeaten start to the Division 1 campaign. The performance also featured contributions from several members of our Under-16s squad. The visitors made a dream start, scoring just 22 seconds after kick-off. A misplaced pass allowed Birmingham to move forward quickly and, after working the ball into the penalty area, they found the net from close range. Chelsea responded positively and began to establish control of possession, with our pressure rewarded in the 38th minute. Keira Johnson set the ball back for Tess Finn, who drove beyond the Birmingham defence before finishing from inside the penalty area to equalise. Four minutes later, the Blues went ahead. Nelly Las and Johnson combined on the right before the latter's cross was cut out. The clearance fell to Maria Mayers on the edge of the area, and she took a touch before firing into the top-left corner and celebrating in style (top). There was still time for another before the break. Straight from kick-off, Las played the ball forward to Ella Abayomi, whose pass across the edge of the penalty area found Gabi Storey. The defender struck first time, sending an excellent effort beyond the goalkeeper to make it 3-1. Chelsea maintained their attacking momentum in the second half, with Abayomi adding her name to the scoresheet five minutes after the restart. Las delivered from the right and Abayomi finished confidently inside the penalty area. Jahmya Putman made it five in the 61st minute. Chloe Sarwie released Aysia Matabaro down the left, and the winger reached the byline before cutting the ball back for Putman to finish first time. A Birmingham defender then turned Sarwie's inswinging corner into her own net in the 66th minute, before Abayomi scored her second two minutes later. Matabaro again provided the delivery, picking out the forward inside the box for a composed finish. Storey then claimed her second of the afternoon in the 75th minute, meeting Las's pass with a shot that flew past the goalkeeper. Birmingham pulled one back a minute later after a long clearance caused problems for the Chelsea defence, allowing their striker to run through and score. The Blues responded with two more goals. Matabaro drove through the penalty area before finishing with her right foot in the 79th minute, following Maria Mayers' pass. The scoring was completed in the 88th minute. Mayers regained possession and found Matabaro on the left, whose cross reached Las. She controlled before shooting, with a deflection helping the ball find the top corner to complete the 10-goal haul. The victory means Chelsea remain unbeaten in PGA Division 1 after four matches, collecting ten points from a possible 12 as we head into the international break. The Blues now take a break from domestic action, with several members of the squad set to represent their countries at Under-17 and Under-19 level. Chelsea return to PGA Division 1 action on Wednesday 9 December, when we travel to face Bristol City.
